en: Thus have I heard: the Mahāmāluṅkyasutta, the sixty-fourth discourse of the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Do you, bhikkhus, remember the five lower fetters taught by me?”
When this was said, the Venerable Māluṅkyaputta said to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I remember the five lower fetters taught by the Blessed One.
“But how, Māluṅkyaputta, do you remember the five lower fetters taught by me?”
“Venerable sir, I remember identity view as taught by the Blessed One as a lower fetter;
I remember doubt as taught by the Blessed One as a lower fetter;
and I remember adherence to rules and observances as taught by the Blessed One as a lower fetter.”
“Venerable sir, I remember sensual desire as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One;
I remember ill will as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One.
It is in this way, venerable sir, that I remember the five lower fetters taught by the Blessed One.”
“Māluṅkyaputta, for whom do you remember these five lower fetters as taught by me?
Will not the wanderers of other sects, Māluṅkyaputta, find fault with you on account of this simile of the infant?
For a young boy, Māluṅkyaputta, who is tender and lies on his back, does not even have the notion of ‘self-existence’ (sakkāya), so how could the view of self-existence arise in him?”
The underlying tendency to the view of personal identity (sakkāyadiṭṭhānusaya) persists in him.
For, Māluṅkyaputta, in a young boy, a tender infant lying on his back, even the word "phenomena" does not exist; how then could doubt regarding phenomena arise in him?
The underlying tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya) persists in him.

For a young, tender infant lying on its back, Māluṅkyaputta, even the notion of "virtue" does not exist; how then could there arise in him a misapprehension of virtue and observances regarding virtues?
Yet the underlying tendency toward the misapprehension of virtue and observances persists within him.
For a young, tender infant lying on its back, Māluṅkyaputta, even the notion of "sensual pleasures" does not exist; how then could there arise in him sensual desire regarding sensual pleasures?
The underlying tendency to sensual lust lies latent within him.
For, Māluṅkyaputta, in a young boy, a tender infant lying on his back, even the notion of "beings" does not exist; how then could ill will toward beings arise in him?
The underlying tendency to ill will lies latent within him.
“Māluṅkyaputta, will not the wanderers of other sects find fault with this by means of this simile of the young man?
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
“Now is the time for this, Blessed One; now is the time for this, Sugata.”
“May the Blessed One teach the five lower fetters; having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.
“Therefore, Ānanda, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:

“In this case, Ānanda, an uninstructed worldling—who has not seen the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who has not seen true persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—dwells with a mind obsessed by the view of personal existence and is led away by the view of personal existence.”
And he does not understand, as it really is, the escape from the arisen view of a personal identity.
That view of a personal identity becomes firmly rooted and is not relinquished; it is a fetter belonging to the lower realm.
He dwells with a mind obsessed by doubt, overcome by doubt.
And he does not understand, as it really is, the escape from arisen doubt.
That doubt becomes firmly rooted and remains unremoved, becoming a fetter pertaining to the lower realm.
He dwells with a mind obsessed by adherence to rules and observances, and is carried away by adherence to rules and observances.
And he does not understand, as it really is, the escape from arisen adherence to rules and observances.
That adherence to rules and observances becomes firmly established and remains unremoved in him as a lower fetter.
He dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual lust, dominated by sensual lust.
And he does not understand, as it really is, the escape from arisen sensual desire.
That sensual desire becomes firmly rooted and remains unremoved, becoming a lower fetter.
He dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will, his mind dominated by ill will.
And he does not understand, as it really is, the escape from arisen ill will.
That ill will of his becomes firmly rooted and is not dispelled; it is a fetter belonging to the lower realm.
But, Ānanda, the well-taught noble disciple, who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones and proficient in the Dhamma of the noble ones...
Well-disciplined, seeing true persons, skilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and well-trained in the Dhamma of true persons,
he does not dwell with a mind obsessed by the view of a personal identity, nor is he overcome by the view of a personal identity;
and he understands, as it really is, the escape from the arisen view of a personal identity.
That identity view of his, along with its underlying tendencies, is abandoned.
He does not dwell with a mind obsessed by doubt, nor one overwhelmed by doubt;
and he understands, as it truly is, the escape from arisen doubt.
His doubt together with its underlying tendency is abandoned.
He does not dwell with a mind obsessed by misapprehension of rules and observances, nor is he possessed by misapprehension of rules and observances;
and he understands, as it really is, the escape from arisen misapprehension of rules and observances.
His adherence to rules and observances, along with its underlying tendency, is abandoned.
He does not dwell with a mind obsessed by sensual lust, nor is he overcome by sensual lust;
and he understands, as it really is, the escape from arisen sensual lust.
His underlying tendency toward sensual lust is abandoned.
He does not dwell with a mind obsessed by ill will, nor is he overcome by ill will;
and he understands, as it really is, the escape from arisen ill will.
That underlying tendency toward ill will in him is abandoned.
Ānanda, without resorting to that path and that way of practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters, one would not know or see those five lower fetters.
‘He will abandon it’—this is impossible.

Ānanda, just as when a great tree stands possessed of heartwood, after its bark has been stripped away and its sapwood has been stripped away, it is impossible that the cutting off of the heartwood will occur [without first removing those layers];
so too, this is impossible.

In the same way, Ānanda, it is impossible that one could know, see, or abandon the five lower fetters without resorting to the path and the practice for the abandoning of those five lower fetters. This is not possible.
But as for the path and the way, Ānanda, by which the five lower fetters are abandoned:
it is possible that, by resorting to that path and that way, one will know, see, or abandon those five lower fetters. This is a possibility.

"Just as, Ānanda, when there is a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, after cutting through the bark and cutting through the sapwood, it is possible that the heartwood will be cut; even so, Ānanda,
by resorting to that path and that way of practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters, one will know or see those five lower fetters."
Or he will abandon it— this is possible.
Just as, Ānanda, the river Gaṅgā might be full of water, level with its banks so that a crow could drink from it,
and then a weak man might come along:
‘I shall swim across the current of this river Ganges by my arms and go safely to the other shore’—
he would not be able to swim across the current of the river Ganges by his arms and go safely to the other shore.
In the same way, Ānanda, when the Dhamma for the cessation of identity is being taught, the minds of certain people do not leap forward, do not find confidence, do not settle, and are not liberated.
Just as that weak man should be regarded, so too are these to be seen.
Ānanda, it is just as if the river Gaṅgā were full of water, brimming to the top so that a crow could drink from it,
and then a strong man were to come along:
‘I shall swim across the current of this river Ganges by the strength of my arms and reach the further shore in safety’—
he would indeed be able to swim across the current of the river Ganges by the strength of his arms and reach the further shore in safety.
In the same way, Ānanda, for whomever the mind leaps forward, gains confidence, becomes settled, and is liberated when the Dhamma is taught for the cessation of identity (sakkāyanirodha).
Just as that strong man [is to be understood], so too should these be seen.
And what, Ānanda, is the path, what is the way for the abandoning of the five lower fetters?
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, through seclusion from acquisitions and through the abandoning of unwholesome states, [is entirely free] from bodily rigidity...
With the subsiding [of applied thought], secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states,
he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
Whatever there is therein belonging to form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—
He contemplates those phenomena as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as an arrow, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien,
as disintegrating, as empty, and as non-self.
He withdraws his mind from those phenomena.
Having turned the mind away from those phenomena, he directs his mind toward the deathless element, thinking:
"This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
Established therein, he attains the destruction of the taints.
If he does not reach the destruction of the taints, then by that very passion for the Dhamma and that delight in the Dhamma,
with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there,
not subject to return from that world. This, Ānanda, is the path, this is the way to the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
Furthermore, Ānanda, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna … the third jhāna … and enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
Thus, whatever there is therein belonging to form, belonging to feeling, belonging to perception, belonging to volitional formations, or belonging to consciousness...
[as before] ...he is no longer subject to returning from that world.
This too, Ānanda, is the path, this is the way for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.

Furthermore, Ānanda, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [a bhikkhu] enters and dwells in the base of infinite space, [perceiving]: "Space is infinite.
Whatever there is therein that pertains to feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness...
...and so on... subject to non-return from that world.
This, Ānanda, is the path, this is the way for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking “consciousness is infinite,” enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.

Whatever there is therein that pertains to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness … [as before] … *Note: The ellipsis indicates the repetition of the standard formula regarding the cessation of those aggregates.*
He is of a nature not to return from that world.
This, Ānanda, is the path, this is the way for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing," enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
Thus, whatever there is therein that pertains to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness...
[as before] ...he is no longer subject to returning from that world.
“This too, Ānanda, is the path, this is the way for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
“If, Bhante, this is the path and this is the way for the abandoning of the five lower fetters, then why is it that here some bhikkhus are liberated by mind and some bhikkhus are liberated by wisdom?
“In this regard, Ānanda, I say there is a difference in their faculties.”
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
The Venerable Ānanda, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Mahā-Mālukya Sutta, the fourth, is concluded.
